title: Streetlights Are Trapping Pill Bugs in Giant Spinning Circles
hook: Thousands of woodlice have been found marching in circular 'death spirals' under streetlights — never seen in the wild before, and a new clue to how light pollution reshapes animal behavior.
key_points: Researchers documented thousands of pill bugs (woodlice) forming synchronized circular 'death spirals' around the edges of streetlight beams.
Individual spirals have contained more than 5,000 animals, moving continuously along the boundary of the illuminated area.
A streetlight's beam creates a sharp circular edge of light on the ground; isopods are drawn to walk along that edge, and the behavior becomes self-sustaining as more join in.
It's the first documented evidence that artificial night lighting can trigger large-scale collective behavior disruption in ground-dwelling animals.
Researchers believe the spirals are harmful traps, leaving pill bugs vulnerable to predators and exhausted, distracted from normal sheltering behavior.
content_html: Artificial light already keeps birds awake and disorients sea turtle hatchlings. Now add pill bugs to the list: researchers have documented thousands of woodlice trapped in synchronized circular "death spirals" under streetlights, a behavior no one had seen in the wild before.
extra_html: A streetlight's beam casts a sharp circular edge of light on the ground, and isopods are drawn to walk along that boundary. As more individuals join the moving perimeter, the behavior becomes self-sustaining — some spirals have contained more than 5,000 animals circling continuously. It's the first documented evidence that artificial night lighting can disrupt collective behavior in ground-dwelling animals at this scale, and researchers see it as a trap rather than anything beneficial: pill bugs caught in the spiral stay exposed to predators and burn energy that would otherwise go toward normal sheltering. It's a small, easy-to-overlook example of how much artificial light may be quietly rewriting animal behavior in ways we're only starting to notice.

flashcards.prompt: What is the pill bug 'death spiral' behavior discovered under streetlights?
flashcards.back_html: Thousands of pill bugs (woodlice) form a synchronized circular formation, continuously walking along the edge of a streetlight's illuminated area — sometimes more than 5,000 animals in one spiral.

flashcards.prompt: What triggers the death spiral behavior?

choices.text: Isopods are drawn to walk along the sharp circular edge of a streetlight's beam, and the behavior becomes self-sustaining as more join
The pill bugs are fleeing from a predator hidden in the light
Streetlight heat draws them into a tight circle for warmth

flashcards.explanation_html: The light creates a defined boundary on the ground; isopods follow that edge, and as more individuals join the moving perimeter, the spiral becomes self-reinforcing.

flashcards.prompt: Why do researchers consider this behavior harmful rather than natural?

choices.text: It leaves the isopods vulnerable to predators and exhausted, distracted from normal sheltering behavior
It causes them to reproduce far more than usual
It helps them find food more efficiently

flashcards.explanation_html: Rather than a beneficial behavior, the spiral appears to be an artificial trap — the animals stay exposed and burn energy instead of sheltering as they normally would.
